title: Harness the Memory: A Holistic Evaluation of Memory Substrates in Memory Agents
claim: Existing evaluations concentrate on a few benchmarks and rarely report efficiency, leaving a gap in broad, cost-aware coverage.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: bar chart, bar chart with inset donut, bubble scatter
description: Three side-by-side plots survey 52 memory-augmented LLM systems. Panel (a) is a vertical bar chart of benchmark usage: LoCoMo 29, LongMemEval 18, Other 22, HotPot/MuSiQue 4, DMR 2, DialSim 1. Each bar has its own color, and italic gray text in the corner gives summary stats. Panel (b) is a horizontal bar chart of the share of systems reporting each metric. Accuracy is 100% and per-type 67%. A dashed divider separates performance metrics (blue) from efficiency metrics (red to tan): any efficiency 21%, latency 12%, token 10%, runtime 4%, memory size 4%, API calls 2%. A donut inset shows GPT family 81% (blue) vs non-GPT 19% (red). Panel (c) is a bubble scatter of number of benchmarks used (x) against number of efficiency metrics reported (y). Blue circles are GPT-family systems and red triangles are non-GPT systems. Bubble size shows system count, and named systems such as LightMem and Mem0 are labeled. Most systems cluster at the bottom left.
caption: Evaluation landscape of 52 memory-augmented LLM systems (2023--2026). (a) Benchmark adoption: 62% of usage concentrates on LoCoMo and LongMemEval. (b) Metric coverage: every system reports accuracy but only 21% report any efficiency metric; 81% of systems use GPT-family backbones. (c) Breadth and efficiency: half of systems use a single benchmark with no efficiency metrics; no system simultaneously achieves broad coverage and comprehensive efficiency reporting.
abstract: Memory is becoming core infrastructure for long-horizon LLM agents, yet existing evaluations offer limited guidance on which memory substrate, namely the underlying medium in which memory is represented and stored, should be used under different operating regimes. We introduce a unified suite of 26 performance and efficiency metrics, including auxiliary-LLM costs attributed to the write, read, and management stages, and apply it identically to 11 memory methods in a controlled harness that varies only the memory substrate. The methods cover dense and sparse indices, text records, structural stores, hierarchical stores, refinement-based memories, parametric updates, and activation-compatible context mechanisms, and we evaluate them with three backbone models on four benchmark suites spanning user-centric question answering and agent-centric decision-making. Our results show that no single substrate consistently dominates: broad retrieval benefits long-context factual QA, while excessive retrieval can harm sequential decision-making by shifting attention away from action-critical context. Scalability introduces a further routing axis, as substrates that perform well at moderate history lengths can become costly or brittle at longer horizons. These regime-dependent reversals make substrate selection a design axis. Choosing a substrate per observable operating regime improves over the best fixed substrate on our benchmarks, while query-level routing leaves most of the oracle headroom open. The findings provide empirical guidance for designing efficient, reliable, and regime-aware long-term memory for LLM agents.
